commenti.body:
I’m in the same boat, we probably watched it on the same streaming service I refuse to name to avoid any kind of unintentional endorsement of a certain media company ran by a penis in a suit.

I was actually pretty blown away revisiting it. I remember liking it; I had it in my brain as a cute little movie with some emotional resonance. But I actually appreciated it a lot more this second time around.

I think the shift in people that results in their “going to color” is a rejection of conformity, accidental or deliberate. That first guy who has sex stays black and white the whole movie, I think because he was just going along with where Reese Witherspoon wanted to take him. That’s why she achieves colorization by reading: she’s rejecting the social pressure of coolness she adhered to in her previous life.

I don’t really share your criticisms. I thought Bud’s development into an agitator happened organically with the story; one example being he noticed the increased happiness of his mom and the Jeff Daniels character. I guess I didn’t feel like anything was missing or that the film was lacking development, plot logic, or resolution; I thought it kinda hit the sweet spot!

While we don’t see eye to eye, thanks for the post! I was actually thinking about asking y’all about this one. I think it is a thoroughly impressive and worthwhile film that deserves to be revisited by young audiences.

It’s a profound movie, in my view. I actually prefer it to The Truman Show, which I see as having a similar theme. I’ve also read descriptions comparing it to Plato’s allegory of the cave.  Here’s a link to a description of that allegory.  http://webspace.ship.edu/cgboer/platoscave.html

“What if there is a world…*outside * of Pleasantville?”   Pleasantville would be like life inside the cave, where one only saw shadows projected on the wall — by analogy, a world in black and white.   Manifesting in color would be like  attaining to *knowledge * of what’s outside of it; even for Plato, the idea of leaving the case was a metaphor for attaining to a greater state of awareness of what lies behind appearances.

There is great beauty to be had — and truth; but also a fear, anxiety, discomfort and disorientation, hesitation, in going from the comfortable and familiar (even if monotone) to the scary and unfamiliar.  For this reason, I actually see “Pleasantville” as similar in theme to both “The Truman Show” and “The Matrix.”

Your analogy of growth is a very good one.   As in Frank Baum’s “Wizard of Oz,” the areas needing growth can vary from person to person.    Toby Maguire’s character lacks courage,  derringer-do.  His mother finds growth in discovering sensuality.  His sister, in her way, is *already* precociously sexual; her growth, instead,  is intellectual.    The waiter at the lunch counter discovers his artistic creativity.  Bud’s father discovers his ability to feel, to express, emotional intimacy. 

I didn’t feel Reese Witherspoon’s character was given short shrift.  When she said “I did the slut thing already; it got kind of tired” it seemed in keeping with this arc of growth.  

Her growth reminds me of Malcolm X in prison, discovering the library. 

      “I spent two days just riffling uncertainly through the dictionary’s pages. I’d never realized so many words existed! I didn’t know which words I needed to learn. Finally, just to start some kind of action, I began copying.
            In my slow, painstaking, ragged handwriting, I copied into my tablet everything printed on that first page, down to the punctuation marks.
            I believe it took me a day. Then, aloud, I read back, to myself, everything I’d written on the tablet. Over and over, aloud, to myself, I read my own handwriting.
            I woke up the next morning, thinking about those words—immensely proud to realize that not only had I written so much at one time, but I’d written words that I never knew were in the world. Moreover, with a little effort, I also could remember what many of these words meant. I reviewed the words whose meanings I didn’t remember. Funny thing, from the dictionary first page right now, that “aardvark” springs to my mind. The dictionary had a picture of it, a long-tailed, long-eared, burrowing African mammal, which lives off termites caught by sticking out its tongue as an anteater does for ants.
            I was so fascinated that I went on—I copied the dictionary’s next page. And the same experience came when I studied that. With every succeeding page, I also learned of people and places and events from history. Actually the dictionary is like a miniature encyclopedia. Finally the dictionary’s A section had filled a whole tablet—and I went on into the B’s. That was the way I started copying what eventually became the entire dictionary. It went a lot faster after so much practice helped me to pick up handwriting speed. Between what I wrote in my tablet, and writing letters, during the rest of my time in prison I would guess I wrote a million words.
            I suppose it was inevitable that as my word-base broadened, I could for the first time pick up a book and read and now begin to understand what the book was saying. Anyone who has read a great deal can imagine the new world that opened.”

These words of Oscar Wilde’s also seem on the wavelength of Pleasantville, and of Reese Witherspoon’s character.

“I don’t regret for a single moment having lived for pleasure. I did it to the full, as one should do everything that one does. There was no pleasure I did not experience. I threw the pearl of my soul into a cup of wine. I went down the primrose path to the sound of flutes. I lived on honeycomb. But to have continued the same life would have been wrong because it would have been limiting. I had to pass on. The other half of the garden had its secrets for me also.”

I think Bud's change works as is, but can be improved by a adding a scene or two, Mary Sue's is very abrupt and I don't think anything really leads to that change. And despite her rejecting Skip to study the next time we see her she is still with him, at the book burning. While she still might be with him after that it doesn't make sense to me that she would be at the riot/book burning event. And her slut shaming herself really comes from no where. I feel like we're missing quite a few scenes after the halfway point. One where Bud has a call to action to become a harbinger of growth. A few with Reese Witherspoon where she is praised for being the Smart Mary Sue, and one where Skip only thinks of her as a subservient girl and not a person, or maybe that she is only good for sex/being a home maker. We are for sure missing a scene where Bud decides he's learned enough to go home as a better person, where I assume his mom disagrees and says she won't say goodbye to him. They also reference a flood and the mural shows town hall sinking. I think that ties into a few comments about danger that hint at a plot line not in the final cut, but we get the climax of Bud punching those boys and gaining his color. 

Too be clear I really like the movie. But there seems to be a lot that hint at a longer more cohesive story, but that was cut down, I imagine to keep it at around 2 hours for a theatrical release. Maybe 140-150 minutes or so as opposed to the 124 minute cut we have. I also had forgotten to mention that the color effects they did were groundbreaking at the time to stick another feather in the cap of this movie so to speak.

I get where you’re approaching this from, but I do disagree in the sense that I think the movie is served by its shorter run time. I think it does require reading between the lines to appreciate the full arcs of the story and some of the characters, but I think it competently and thoroughly lays the groundwork to allow a comprehensive reading. I like how Mary Sue sort of takes a backseat after she serves her function as initial instigator, and I think we’re given all the details and character beats to flesh out her journey on our own. I guess I’m appreciating it as a throw back to when a movie was expected to be 90-120 minutes; I appreciate how story economy can focus a film.

I actually just rewatched it a few days ago and I felt like it didn't hold up at all and didn't match my positive memories at all. It's horribly paced/rushed with no real stakes outside of the foundational concept. It's not very well acted even though the cinematography and set design is very well done. It never felt like anything that was happening mattered outside of having a dramatic score. Nothing was developed and the story relied way too much on traditional tropes to impact the audience. I was really let down upon revisiting it.
